question: Following demands from drug manufacturers, the Nea Dimokratia government has announced large increases of up to 357% in the prices of more than 400 pharmaceutical products in Greece. This decision adds pressure on the already high cost of pharmaceutical care for the population and brings new profits for drug manufacturers.

This is a criminal policy which historically has been supported by all Greek governments implementing decisions of the EU, a recent case being the pharmaceutical package voted in by the European Parliament in April 2024, which established new incentives, privileges and concessions for the pharmaceutical groups, while the public are forced to live in insecurity and their health is sacrificed.

Low-income households will be further burdened with an increase in the cost of insurance, and the government’s obligation to ensure prompt provision of medicines free of charge will be shifted still further towards people’s ‘personal responsibility’, with incalculable consequences for public health. In view of this, what is the Commission’s view on the following: 1.

the fact that the implementation of the EU strategy in all Member States, treating medicines as a commodity, demonstrably places a further burden on working people, who are left to face medicine shortages, all in the name of supporting the profitability and competitiveness of drug companies?
the demand to abolish all payments and contributions by patients for all medicines, since they should be a common good and not a commercial commodity?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.9.2024) 1. EU actions in the field of medicines serve numerous objectives, recognising the crucial role of medicines for public and patient health.

The Pharmaceutical Strategy for Europe1 and the reform of the EU pharmaceutical legislation2 aim at balancing several main objectives, including access to medicines, competitiveness of the EU pharmaceutical sector, as well as affordability of medicines for both patients and healthcare systems.

The Commission’s reform proposal aims at facilitating earlier entry of generic and biosimilar medicines to improve affordability of medicines, at increasing the availability of comparative clinical data to support more evidence-based decisions on pricing, and at increasing the transparency of public funding for research and development of medicines.

The proposal also contains measures aimed at enhancing the security of supply and preventing shortages of medicines. The European Parliament and the Council are currently discussing the reform, and the importance of those objectives is acknowledged by all three EU institutions.

It remains that pricing and reimbursement decisions regarding medicines fall under the competence of the Member States and are based on national considerations on the allocation of national health budgets.

To enhance affordability of medicines, the Commission promotes cooperation between national authorities, through exchange of information and best practices on national pricing, reimbursement and procurement policies. 2.

Notwithstanding the actions enhancing affordability of medicines described in point 1, as already mentioned, pricing and reimbursement of medicines are a national competence, and the way Member States regulate in this area is outside the remit of EU law.
